segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: A few weeks ago, I talked to a woman named Melissa Salpietra. She's pregnant, so she had a lot on her mind. But the thing she was obsessing over most-- more than baby names, or strollers, or the new house she and her husband recently bought-- was this package that had arrived in the mail with her name on it.

And if I open it up and there's a pair of pants in it, I'm going to have a boy. But if I open it up and there is a little pink dress, I'm going to be having a girl.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Now I've never been pregnant before. And I don't have kids. But it's my impression that this is not how an unborn baby's sex is normally determined.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: From what I understand, there are these things called chromosomes and then some procedure known as a sonogram. But in Melissa's family, they don't bother with that stuff. Instead--

segments.speaker: Melissa
segments.text: You get sent the prediction of your sex in the mail. You get not even the prediction, you get sent the foretelling of what you're going to have, a boy or a girl.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: This is a longstanding tradition in Melissa's family. Three generations have participated in it, more than 20 babies. Family legend is the prediction has been right every time.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: It all began more than 35 years ago with Melissa's great-grandmother, Carmela Calanni, AKA, Nonna. Nonna had moved here from Sicily when she was a teenager. She made her living as a seamstress.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: She was quiet, unassuming. She baked bread, and made lasagna from scratch, and went to church every day. But Melissa says there was more to Nonna than met the eye.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Hoping to nail that job interview? Talk to Nonna. Trying to buy a new house? Go see Nonna. She didn't even make you kiss her hand.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: So years before Melissa was born, when one of Nonna's grandsons announced that his wife was expecting a baby, he went to Nonna and asked for a little favor. He told her he wanted a boy. Here's Melissa's mom, Mary Annette, who was around at the time.

segments.text: Now Nonna was nine for nine. The statistical odds of getting the prediction right that many times are less than 1 in 500. Not to mention the fact that she predicted a boy girl set of twins.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: And all of this rocketed Nonna from regular old clairvoyant grandma status to legend. The pants and the dress became an institution. Even after Nonna died in 1999, they kept working.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Kids who'd been predicted themselves the first time around were now having kids of their own. And Nonna kept getting it right. As the years went on, pants/dress protocol was codified.

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: For instance, if someone else got pregnant while you were pregnant, you could not send them your garment until you had your baby. You had to wait until you stitched your child's name onto the pants or the dress. It's just the way it was done.

segments.text: And there were some close calls. There was one rogue baby, where the parents received neither the pants nor the dress. They had a boy.

segments.text: I went through the family tree. And it turns out that of 21 predictions, Nonna was wrong two times. Most family members were vague about this. They kind of had a sense that something might have gone awry a couple times. But they were hazy on the details.

segments.text: Or maybe it was because these two girls were the last kids in their generation. Nonna was at the end of her life when they were born and died not long after. It's possible her powers were diminished.

segments.speaker: Woman 5

segments.speaker: Melissa's Mom
segments.text: I feel like I'm waiting for the smoke, and the pope, and the whole thing. [LAUGHS].

segments.speaker: Brian Reed
segments.text: Finally, she could wipe the sweat off her brow and breathe a sigh of relief. Not only was she getting the boy she wanted, she could call Nonna's relatives all over the country without shame or disappointment and tell them that number 23 was right.

segments.speaker: Melissa
segments.text: Laura.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is another story of people communicating not with words but with an inanimate object. Dave Hill has been on our show from time to time. He's a comedian and a musician.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He told this story onstage at Cameo Gallery in Brooklyn. A warning for the squeamish, he mentions pee in here.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: This is something that happened to me a few weeks ago right here in town. But backing things up a little bit. I moved here to New York in 2003 from Cleveland. Thank you!

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: [LIGHT APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Thank you. Anyway, the time that I've been here-- maybe you guys can relate to this, too-- all I ever hear is, New York used to be so edgy. But now it's lost its edge. It's not edgy anymore.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Because I understand that there was a time in New York when you could walk down the street, and just crack open a beer, and just suck it down, and throw the bottle on the ground.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And you might get, like, a little raped, or whatever.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But it didn't matter. It was like a give and take. You took the good with the bad. And everyone was fine with it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And now you can't really get away with any of that stuff. But you can get a really nice brunch at a lot of places. Just go with your friends, free refills on mimosas. It's great for everybody.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the reason I bring this up is a few weeks ago I was doing a show out here in Brooklyn. It was a very classy show with all these people, and a sold out show. So I put on a fancy suit. And I spent, like, six to eight hours on my hair.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the people putting the show on were like, oh, Dave, you've got to get out here on time. So I'm rushing to get out there. And I'm at 28th and Broadway. And the R train's right there.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So I'm like, oh, I'll take the R train. That's like a reputable train. And right before I'm going to go on the subway, I realize, oh, I'm so hungry. And then I look. And there's a gyro car right there.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So I go to the gyro guy. I'm like, give my a gyro. And then he's got all the sauces, like the yogurt sauce, and the chili sauce, and the garlic sauce. And I'm just like, sauce the [BLEEP] out of that thing. And don't hold back on me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And he just starts just hosing down the gyro. Like, calm down. And then finally, he gives me the gyro.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I go down into the subway. And the train comes right away. I get on it with the gyro. I start eating the gyro. And the sauces just start dripping all over my hands, and on the ground, and on my shoes and everything. And it's rush hour. And the train's, like, super crowded, and everything.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I'm realizing, oh, I'm probably stinking up the whole car with this gyro. And people are probably looking at me thinking, that guy looks incredible. But it's not very cool what he's doing with that gyro.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So I'm thinking the best thing that I can do for everyone on the train, and for the city of New York in general, is just get off the subway at the next stop, finish the gyro, get back on, go out to Brooklyn. And so I get off at the next stop, 23rd Street. Lightning quick decision.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then I walk all the way to the end of the platform to eat my gyro. Because I don't even want to bother anyone on the platform with my gyro. I do cool [BLEEP] like this all the time.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so I go all the way down to the end of the platform. And you know how at the end of the subway they have the black metal storage bins? Not like a Norwegian black metal storage, which would be so cool. It's just like a regular black metal storage, almost like a dumpster or something.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So I'm stand next to it. And I've finished my gyro. And then I have the wrapper. And I'm looking around for a trash can to throw it out. And there's no trash can anywhere on the whole platform.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it's too messy to put in my pocket. And I'm like, oh, I don't want to throw it on the ground. I don't want to throw it on the track.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So I think the best thing that I can do in this scenario is just set it down on the black metal storage bin. That way, whoever has to clean it up later, they don't have to bend over. They can just kind of swoop it into the satchel. I might be kind of fun for them. I don't even know.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so I set it down. And as soon as I do, I start to hear this rustling, and rumbling, and [GROWLING SOUNDS]. And it turns out there's this homeless guy sort of camped out on the other side of the storage bin. And I woke him up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And he's like this sleeping giant, just like, [GROWLING SOUNDS]. And he gets up. And his bones are creaking. And his hair is, like, all crazy all over the place. And he looks at me. And he just starts yelling. And he's like, back up! Back up!

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I move like a little bit. But I'm like, what's this guy going to do? So I don't really move that much.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But then he's like, back up! And get this trash out of here. And he smacks the trash out at me. And I'm like, that's rude.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then he screams again. He's like, back up! Back up! And this guy, like, he was seriously homeless. It wasn't like a phase he was going through, where he's like, oh, that's Don. I'm sure he'll be back up in his place any day now. He is like this seriously crazy, caveman homeless guy.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So it occurs to me. It's like, this might not even be about me. He might be yelling at some other guy, imaginary guy, who's just like standing exactly where I'm standing. So I'm still not really moving.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So I'm like, oh, the train's coming, whatever. And then he goes, back up or I'll throw this bottle of piss on you! And then from out of nowhere, like a ninja, all of a sudden he's got this Gatorade bottle.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it's a huge Gatorade bottle. It's not like the size you get, like, oh, hang on, I'm just going to the store to get some Gatorade. It's like the giantest size. The kind you drink if you're like, I only drink Gatorade. It's like huge, the hugest size. Only, instead of being full of delicious and refreshing Gatorade, it's full of pee, of urine.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And just real quick, has anyone here ever peed in a bottle before?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [APPLAUSE]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, yeah. Of course. But yeah, I was just doing it before.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But the reason I bring it up is if you haven't peed in a bottle before, you think when you have to go really bad you're like, oh my God, I just went like nine gallons. It was crazy. But we don't, as humans-- and you know this if you've peed in a bottle-- we actually don't pee that much.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now the reason I bring it up is because to fill a huge Gatorade bottle, that's like a week or two's worth of urine. Now if you factor in that the homeless are a historically dehydrated people, this is like three or four weeks of pee saved up.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And he's just like, back up or I'll throw this bottle of piss on you! And the way I'm saying it, it sounds like he's like, back up. That's the first option. And if you choose not to do that, I'll throw this bottle of urine that I just happen to have. I'll throw it on you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But he doesn't say it like that at all. He's just like, back up or I'll throw this bottle of piss on you. And before he even finishes his sentence, he cocks his arm back and just launches it at me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [AUDIENCE GASPS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I know!

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And oh my God, homeless or not, like, not a drop wasted. His aim was incredible. It was just coming right at me. The first blow nails me right in the head. Like all my hair, all that work for nothing. My hair is totally ruined.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's going down my back and down my jacket. And it's soaking my pants. It soaks through my pants, soaks my underwear. He had effectively wet my pants with his pee.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And at this point in the story, I'm getting a bit irritated, right? And I'm thinking to myself, well, Dave, what would you do if a total stranger drenched you in his own pee? And up to that point in my life I would have thought like, oh, I'd kill that guy, and hurt his feelings, and really give him a real stern talking to.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But that wasn't my reaction at all. I was just like, I am getting the [BLEEP] out of here immediately. Because if you figure if your opponent's first move in a confrontation is to just drench you in his own pee, like, what's next? At the very least, he's got a couple more bottles of pee back there, you figure.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So I'm just like, all right, touche. You won this round, well played. I'm getting out of here.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so I walk out of the subway station. And I walk up onto the street. And it's still light outside. And I'm walking down Fifth Avenue.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I start thrashing around to get the pee off of me. And I'm like Jennifer Beals in hit movie, Flashdance . And it's flying all over. And then the sort of rivulets of hobo pee are running down my face and neck, and down my chest and everything.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And I'm looking up. And I see that. And the sun is kind of going through the droplets of pee. And it's forming these beautiful prisms and rainbows. And I'm just transfixed by them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And all of a sudden, all that pain and anger just fell away. Because it was in that moment I realized, this mother [BLEEP] town is back.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [APPLAUSE AND CHEERS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Dave Hill, he's the author of the book Tasteful Nudes, and Other Misguided Attempts at Personal Growth and Validation.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up, our program has been on the radio for over a decade. And finally, finally we have somebody in the second half of today's program for the first time ever who actually has a great voice for radio. I know you've been wondering if this would ever happen. And yes, it is not one of our contributors. It is one of their dads.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio and Public Radio International when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Each week on our program, of course, we choose a theme, bring you different kinds of stories on that theme. Today's program, "Send a Message," stories of messages sent and received, many of them not using words, or words that mean something different than what they're saying.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We have arrived at Act Three of our program. Act Three, "Soul Sister." Sometimes the impressiveness of the messenger is part of what makes a message so powerful. Sonari Glinton has an example of that.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: In the late 1970s, my family moved to a Chicago neighborhood called South Shore. Black families had been moving there for decades. And of course, as we moved in, all the white families moved out.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Which wasn't so bad, partly because when all those white families fled, they left behind all kinds of cool stuff-- golf courses, a few marinas, a gigantic country club, mansions. Mostly, though, they left behind their churches and synagogues.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: One of those churches was my own, Saint Philip Neri Parish. It is a huge church. And it was also my grade school. Right there on 72nd Street, Saint Philip Neri was the beginning and end of my little Catholic universe. Between school, mass on Sundays, basketball, summer camp, I essentially spent my entire childhood there.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: By the time I was in third grade, Saint Philip Neri's students were nearly all black. And just about half of our teachers were black. Each year, more and more black teachers replaced the white ones.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: South Shore was kind of the same. There were just a few white families left. Sometimes during recess, we'd hear bagpipes coming from the church near the playground and watch as groups of white people left the funeral mass.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: But it wasn't just South Shore. Chicago was going through this gigantic change, too. Race was at the forefront of everything. In 1983, Chicago elected its first black mayor, Harold Washington, whose opponents tried to scare voters about a black man holding the job.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Harold Washington's election meant a lot to South Shore. It still does. In 1983, Lou's Barber Shop on 71st Street had a poster of Harold Washington hanging up. Lou's still has that picture of Harold.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: But Harold was just the beginning. Soon after his election, Michael Jordan came to town, then Oprah. In 1984, Jesse Jackson-- the dude from our neighborhood-- was running for president.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: But all of that was going on around us. The biggest thing for me happened at Saint Philip Neri. And it happened with Sister Rosemary Brennan.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Sister Rosemary was the principal at Saint Philip Neri. And principal is such a limp title, when I think about it. Because really, Sister Rosemary was the school. Her presence was big, even though by the fourth grade, I was taller than her.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Sister Rosemary wasn't a nun out of central casting. She'd clearly been a beautiful woman when she was younger. But she didn't wear a habit. She did carry a rosary. She was very Irish, serious, not angry.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Mainly, she took each of us seriously, which came across as love. Her love was fierce. She knew every single kid, every parent. Everything about each of us mattered.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Sister Rosemary didn't talk about race. But what she did, that's a story.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: It was sometime after Christmas break. I was in the fourth grade in my reading class. I had Miss Sperling. It seems important to note that she was white.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Anyway, we were sitting in reading class. So we're all broke up in groups. And in walks Sister Rosemary. Now Sister Rosemary didn't just walk into a classroom for no reason. Either one of the kids or the teacher was in big trouble.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: So everyone stopped what they were doing. And she said, as she would always say, good morning boys and girls. And we said what we would always say, well, sing. Good morning, Sister Rosemary.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: And then Sister Rosemary told us to go back to our work, which was a perfectly silly thing to say. Because when Sister Rosemary was in your class, you paid attention to Sister Rosemary. Even the kindergartners knew that. So our eyes stayed on Sister Rosemary as she grabbed the chair, dragged it across the floor to the front of the room. Then she stood on top of the chair with her back to the class.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: In our classroom, just like in every classroom, there was a crucifix. The crucifix had a blond wooden cross with a figure of Christ suspended on it. Then with her back to the class, Sister Rosemary teetered on her tippy toes, firmly grabbed the bottom of the crucifix, and took it off the wall.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: By this point, no one was reading or even pretending to pay attention to anything else. She placed the cross aside, reached up, again on her tiptoes, and replaced the old crucifix with a new one. And on this cross was a black Jesus. He was carved out of dark wood with a short 'fro, wide nose, full lips, and the same down-turned face as the white Jesus.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: This little Irish woman straightened the cross, adjusted herself, climbed down off the chair, and began to leave the room. All of us were completely silent. Then one brave soul asked her what she was doing.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Without hesitation, Sister Rosemary turned around to us and said, boys and girls, we're not sure what Jesus looked like. But we know he probably looked more like you than like me. Then Sister Rosemary turned around and walked out of the classroom. That was it. No deep discussion. No sitting down and going over it.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: In one moment, she turned Jesus from white to black. Kind of like, OK, boys and girls, Jesus is black. Deal with it on your own.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Sister Rosemary must have done the exact same thing in all the other classes, because from then on, all the crucifixes in our classrooms were black. I can imagine her starting out the day with a full box of black crucifixes and ending it with a bunch of white ones she had to put in storage.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: There were 20 or so classes. So she would have replaced the white crucifix more than 20 times. Each time getting on her tiptoes. Each time meeting the stunned reaction. Each time saying the same thing.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: She could have done it on a Saturday or during a break. But she did it while we were all there. She made the change, not the janitor or the teacher, Sister Rosemary.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Here's the funny thing. No sooner had she switched the crosses that I made the switch in my head. Just like that, Jesus was black. Didn't ponder it. No rolling it over in my head. It made perfect sense to me.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Everything and every one around me was black. So Jesus must have been, too. And plus, Sister Rosemary said so. The rest of my time at Saint Philip Neri, whenever I came across a white Jesus on a worksheet or in our religion book, I took out my pencil or crayon and colored him in to look like me.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: When you're a fourth grader, everything is bigger than you. Everyone is smarter than you, older. But when one day you realize that Jesus is just like you, Jesus is black, then everything short of Jesus seems possible.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Even now when I close my eyes to pray, it's to a Jesus with curly hair and dark skin. That's probably the way it ought to be. Theologically speaking, I know it does not matter at all what color Jesus was. Who he is transcends what he looked like.

segments.speaker: Sonari Glinton
segments.text: Scholars say the historical Jesus probably looked much like the people who live in the Middle East now, just shorter. Probably not much taller than Sister Rosemary. She knew exactly how God should look in my eyes. And luckily enough for me, she was able to show me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sonari Glinton, his regular job, he's a reporter for NPR News.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [MUSIC-- "PERSONAL JESUS," BY  NINA HAGEN]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Four, "Not My First Time at the Rodeo."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There are conversations that you have with your parents that just stay with you your whole life-- what they said, what you said, back and forths that you know by heart. You repeat them to explain who you are to somebody else, or to yourself, and who your parents were. But what if you could re-hear that dialogue decades later? Not your memory of it, but the actual words that were truly spoken. Nancy Updike has this story.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Bill Lahey was in his early 20s and on the phone with his father in 1978 when he heard a faint pinging sound on the phone. He mentioned it. And his father said--

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: When did that start?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: It's been there all along.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: I never heard it.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: No?

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Must be my bad ear.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: There's a ping, like, every five seconds.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Well, that's funny.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Maybe we're being eavesdropped on.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Monitored or something.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Yeah. Sometimes I wonder if this phone is tapped.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Two decades later, after his father had died, Bill was at his dad's house in Ohio cleaning out the office.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: And I opened up a file cabinet and found 30 or 40 cassette tapes with his unmistakable handwritten notations of names and dates. And I knew instantly what they were, that he had been surreptitiously taping us.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Even at the time his father was recording, Bill had guessed what could be going on. It was the kind of thing his father might do. And he did. He recorded hours of calls with Bill.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: And according to his own handwritten labels, he also taped his four other children, his wife, his mother, other relatives, his priest. He recorded calls at home and in the car.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Recording test number four. Road noise, average to low. Speed, 60 miles an hour.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: From the dates on the cassettes, Bill figured they were an archive of his father trying to get the people around him on to his side. Bill's mother had left his father after 37 years of marriage. Bill remembered the gist and tone of those conversations pretty well. They were memorable. And he put off listening to the recordings of them.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: For 12 years, they sat in a black nylon duffel bag that he would move every time the family moved. This was a pile of information Bill wasn't sure he wanted from an era of his life he knew he didn't want to relive.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: He'd sided with his mom in the divorce even before the divorce. Since junior high, he'd been lobbying her to leave his dad. As Bill saw his father, he was smart, tenacious, and a tremendous bully with a bad quick temper and huge blowups. He got worse over time. And he was worse when he drank.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: What Bill remembered from the taped conversations were long calls where his father bullied him and he fought back hard. He saw himself as his mother's advocate and protector.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: I remember him trying to recruit me in his campaign to keep his marriage together. And so my memory was me saying versions of, look, she doesn't want to do that anymore. You guys have tried for a long time. Let it go. You know, some version of face facts, it's over.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: So you remember pushing back verbally, arguing with him?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Yeah, yeah. All the time.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: After those 12 years of holding on to the tapes, Bill finally reached just about the age his father had been when he'd made the recordings. And suddenly Bill wanted to hear them. He felt ready but nervous.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Here was raw data about what I actually did in conversations with my dad. And I just took one of the tapes with me, with my name on, and went into our car in the back of our house. Partially because it was the only place that had a cassette tape recorder that I knew of.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: And the first thing that came on was his voice pretty aggressively questioning me about something. And his voice was as clear as the day I heard it.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: So you got pretty involved there, didn't you, for somebody who didn't want to take sides?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Yeah, I did. Certainly did.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: His father was talking about the fact that Bill and his four siblings all sided with their mother in the divorce in one way or another.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: So why did you do it? What, were you feeling sorry for your mother?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: For being oppressed? You'd think she was going around in a wheelchair. How would you feel, Bill? And have that kind of a situation where the mother hen is being protected. From who?

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: She's got everybody believing that I'm a goddamn bully. She's so psychotic that she's got everybody believing that I'm a bastard. That's how psychotic she is. How would you feel if you were me, Bill?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: And I listened for probably two minutes. And I was like, OK. That's what they are. This is just really intense. I took the tape out, went back and went into the house and told my wife about it. And didn't listen to them again for, I don't know, three or four months.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: When Bill went back to listening for real, what he heard was his father pushing one main point with him hour after hour. Which was, how about you talking your mother into trying again?

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: How do you feel about that assessment?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: To give it a try?

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: [SIGHS]. Well, just from talking to mother over the months, I see no real sign of changing her mind.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: But has anybody really tried to, Bill, forcibly, persuasively? Is it fair that she doesn't try, whether she wants to or not? And the answer, obviously, is no it isn't fair. To have it go down the drain and lose the war for a few battles without trying is, to me, absurd.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Yeah. Well, I guess because I see it more than just a few battles.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: No, I said there was a bunch of them. What the hell's the difference? There were a lot of good times. Why do you look at the black part?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Well, Dad, because I didn't that time that things worked well. I mean, maybe when I was very young.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: You have no-- remember anything? We had no happiness, Bill?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: I didn't say none.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: You just said you never saw the times when we did.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: A period. I mean, when I say things, you know, just generally.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Oh, well, you have a short memory, Bill. I'm sorry to say that. We used to go up to Lake Erie. We had a lot of good times.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: I'm not saying we didn't.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Bill, are you saying that there's no use trying?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: I'm not saying that. I just--

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: What's the bottom line? Let's get down to it. This is a lot of conversation. Tell me what your attitude is. Are you advocating that we don't try?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: I'm just taking--

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: No, I want to know.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Why do you take so long to answer?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Kind of like, say something. You know, just don't sit there. I was less confrontational than I remember or expected. But I could remember that thought process that I went through.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: You know, if I say X, he's going to blow up. If I say, Y, I'm going to throw my mom under the bus.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: I know what Mother's-- at least from what she tells me, this has been something that she's obviously been thinking about a long time.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Not no long time. Maybe four or five years. Bill, do you know that her mind might be affected? And she may not be herself psychologically.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Four or five years?

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Bill, do you realize that her mind might affected? She may not be herself psychologically.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: But for that long of time?

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Yes. Would you like to see us happy if we can arrange to be together?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: Why don't you say that?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Where was the warrior in me? Where was the stand up person that was willing to call a lie a lie, you know, willing to draw bright lines and say, I won't even put up with having a conversation about this?

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: And some of these conversations go on so long. I mean, 45 minutes, an hour. And he's just hammering away at you and at the points he's making. Why did you stay on such a long time? Why not just say, Dad, I got to go?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Yeah. So I was living in Wisconsin during a lot of this taping. I felt badly that my mom was back there, basically by herself dealing with him. And I think I had some notion that by staying on the phone with him, you know, it's like a little bit of the rodeo clown. You know, those old rodeo clowns would be sent out. The cowboy would be bucked off the bull.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: To distract the bull?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Would go out to distract the bull.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Bill wasn't crushed by the difference between what he heard on the tapes and the tough line he'd remembered taking with his dad. But it did throw him off balance. He really had seen himself from the time he was a kid as a warrior standing up to the strong, protecting the weak, a sort of superhero when it came to arguing against his dad.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: But I was less heroic. It was like I was more pragmatic. It was less of an epic struggle of right and wrong and more mundane than that.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I mean, what kid fantasizes about being a pragmatist?

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: [LAUGHS]. Right.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Bill says his mother thrived after the divorce. His father, he says, stayed more or less the same. He married again, divorced again.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Bill kept up a relationship with him his whole life. That had been his other goal during these calls. Besides protecting his mom, not losing his dad. He had thought about that even during the worst arguments. Better a long silence than words he couldn't take back.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Bill saw his father once or twice a year every year after the divorce. And he spoke to him by phone every few weeks until he died.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: I'll call you back soon. Or you could call me in the evening.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: So your number's the same.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: Sure.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: All right.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: And any time you want to chat.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: All right.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: OK. So I will talk to you soon.

segments.speaker: Bill's Father
segments.text: OK, I'm glad you called. Take care.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: OK, Dad. Good night.

segments.speaker: Bill
segments.text: [CLICK]
